title: ALERT: PM Modi Wants a Record of Every Child From Age 3
summary: PM Modi wants a record of every child's activities from age 3, ending in an "aptitude certificate" by Class 10 or 12. Is it a smart way to find hidden talent, or a privacy problem waiting to happen? At IIT Kharagpur's 75th anniversary, Prime Minister Narendra Modi proposed a data and analytics system where parents, teachers and even friends keep adding to a child's record from age three, so that by Class 10 or 12 it shows what the child is naturally good at. In this explainer, Siddhanth and Ravi break down what he actually proposed (he didn't say "AI" or "app"), why he wants it, how much of it already exists through the NEP's Holistic Progress Card and the APAAR student ID, and the big privacy questions under India's new data law. ⏱️ Chapters 0:00 Intro 0:45 The Idea 1:24 Why He Wants It 2:01 Already Half-Built 2:35 The Privacy Question 3:16 Would It Work? 📌 Key numbers • Age 3: when the proposed record would start • ₹15,000–20,000: what Modi said parents pay career counsellors • 26 crore+: APAAR student IDs created by July 2026 • Under 18: a "child" under the DPDP Act, needing a parent's verifiable consent • May 2027: when most DPDP obligations apply Should India track children's aptitude from age 3? Is it a smart way to find hidden talent, or a privacy problem waiting to happen?

At IIT Kharagpur's 75th anniversary, Prime Minister Narendra Modi proposed a data and analytics system where parents, teachers and even friends keep adding to a child's record from age three, so that by Class 10 or 12 it shows what the child is naturally good at. In this explainer, Siddhanth and Ravi break down what he actually proposed (he didn't say "AI" or "app"), why he wants it, how much of it already exists through the NEP's Holistic Progress Card and the APAAR student ID, and the big privacy questions under India's new data law.

title: Get certified now with H2O.ai University
The Benchmark Paradox
summary: When a model achieves a new level on a leaderboard, what does that number actually mean? A benchmark auditor, a user researcher, and a SWE-bench co-author all read benchmark leaderboards, and none of them trusts the number at a glance. In this episode of Beyond the Leaderboard, host Janie Gu talks with three people close to AI benchmarks about what a score won't show you. Run the same tests on different infrastructure and the score changes because the benchmark measures the sandbox, not just the model. Frontier models can now recall entire repositories, which could lead to looking up answers instead of reasoning them. How can benchmark leaderboards remain relevant if all of the answers are known? 🎙️ GUESTS: • Florian Brand, Research Engineer, Prime Intellect • Ofir Press, Research Scientist, co-author of SWE-bench • Matthew Reynolds, Senior User Researcher, Kaggle Hosted by Janie Gu, Group Product Manager, Kaggle Beyond the Leaderboard explores the strategies, surprises, and real stories driving the Kaggle community and the AI industry. ⏱️ CHAPTERS: 0:00 Why benchmark experts don't trust the score 2:46 Where a benchmark number goes wrong 5:02 How a harness changes the score 8:36 Models that cheat by looking up answers 10:58 How to trust a number you can't check 13:03 Public vs private benchmarks 17:33 Why SWE-bench was open source 20:18 Models that memorize whole repositories 23:36 What comes after crawling GitHub 25:25 How a benchmark gets retired 28:47 What benchmarks should measure next 📖 GO DEEPER 🏆 Kaggle Benchmarks: https://www.kaggle.com/benchmarks ▶️ Ofir Press on SWE-bench: https://youtu.be/ubwAgxjEV1A 🖥️ Terminal-Bench: https://www.tbench.ai/ 🛠️ SWE-bench: https://www.swebench.com/ Kaggle is the leading platform for crowdsourced benchmarks, competitions, and hackathons where the community shapes real-world progress in AI. title: Companies Know What AI Costs But Not What It Buys
summary: In this episode, we’re joined by J.R. Storment, Executive Director of the Tokenomics Foundation and the FinOps Foundation at the Linux Foundation, to dig into the question every AI-heavy company is now facing: you know what you’re spending, but can you prove what you’re getting for it? J.R. explains what tokenomics really means (and why it has nothing to do with crypto). The real cost of AI goes well beyond API tokens. It includes harnesses, idle compute, storage, data, and the people who build and run it all. We look at how companies like Canva have had to rethink pricing as AI usage eats into cost of goods sold, flipping the old idea that more engagement is always good news. J.R. also shares findings from a survey of around 500 large enterprises. Most were confident they could see their spend, but 75% couldn’t show value their CFO would defend. Along the way, we cover engineers caught building their next startup on the company’s AI budget, why spend caps can actually push teams toward better decisions, the gap between activity metrics like merged PRs and real business value, why CFOs avoid the term ROI, and how model routing can backfire by breaking your cache. We also get into why not every problem needs an LLM, and how power shortages at data centers are quietly pushing up the cost of AI for everyone downstream. title: In an AI World, the Lab Matters More Than Ever
summary: "My style of physics has always been to go down to the basement and fool around with something and poke this and poke that and try stuff." Professor Peter Taborek is an experimental condensed matter physicist at the University of California, Irvine, and he mentions that he has followed his curiosity wherever it went. He was a student at Caltech, in the same class as Stephen Wolfram. He went on to Bell Labs, working under Nobel laureate Doug Osheroff in the days when a telephone company paid for fundamental research, and then to Texas Instruments, where he grew diamonds from a plasma at a time when many people doubted that was possible. At UC Irvine, he has studied quantum fluids and filmed cilia only a thousand angstroms wide beating around frog embryos. Along the way, Mathematica became one of his most important tools: he got one of the very first licenses on a NeXT computer, and computer algebra let him do calculations he could never have done by hand. Professor Taborek also cares a great deal about how science is taught. He found that the standard mathematical methods textbooks "basically ignored computers," so he wrote his own course, in which students work through problems in computational notebooks and learn to explain their results clearly, because in his view most of a scientist's career is communication. Now that AI "has read every book in the library and it's done every homework problem known to man," he thinks the human part of science is changing. He uses AI and is enthusiastic about it, but he doesn't think it replaces hands-on contact with the physical world, and he believes the lab "down in the basement" is where much of the action will be. His advice to young scientists who are anxious about the future is simple: "I think it's going to be okay."

title: NVIDIA Kumo: Foundation Models for Tabular Data (with Stanford Prof. Jure Leskovec)
summary: #NVIDIAKumo #TabularFoundationModels #GraphNeuralNetworks In Episode #1047, Jure Leskovec (Professor of Computer Science at Stanford and co-founder of Kumo AI, now part of NVIDIA) joins @JonKrohnLearns to explain how a foundation model that has never seen real data can beat hand-built models on enterprise tables. These models need no feature engineering and no training. Jure pioneered graph neural networks, and since NVIDIA acquired Kumo, his team has released the full Kumo family as open weights under a license that allows commercial use. In this episode, Jure breaks down the four Kumo models for tabular, relational, forecasting and anomaly-detection tasks, explains how they are pre-trained on synthetic data, describes how Biomni came to be used by more than 10,000 scientists within weeks and lays out why he believes human judgment has never been more valuable. title: The brain helped us build AI. Now AI is explaining the brain.
summary: The human brain remains one of the greatest unsolved mysteries in science. title: HUGE: Jio Plans 1,600 Satellites to Take On Starlink
summary: Reliance Jio wants its own space internet: about 1,600 satellites, ideally launched on Indian rockets. Siddhanth and Ravi break down Jio's plan, the rocket problem in its way, and the race with Elon Musk's Starlink. According to a report in Mint, Jio Platforms is planning a low Earth orbit constellation of around 1,600 satellites, with a first test launch targeted around September 2027 and the full network by 2035. title: Harness Adapters: Train Your Model for Any Coding Agent
summary: Hugging Face's harness adapters are small LoRA add-ons trained with reinforcement learning for one coding agent. With thinking off, the pi adapter takes Qwen 3.8 27B from 39% to about 65% on the hardest 51 SWE-bench Pro tasks. I explain how a harness adapter works, how you could train your own (RL inside the real agent, hidden tests, a fewer-steps bonus, and the safeagents guard against reward hacking), and what happened when I tested it on two DGX Sparks against the plain model and maximum thinking. LINKS: Hugging Face harness-hub: https://huggingface.co/harness-hub Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted (model card): https://huggingface.co/harness-hub/Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted Blog, "Harness adapters: Safe RL for efficient agentic development": https://huggingface.co/blog/harness-hub/harness-adapters safeagents plugin: https://huggingface.co/harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin Training script (TRL, examples/async_grpo_harbor): https://github.com/huggingface/trl pi coding agent: https://pi.dev RELATED VIDEOS: I Trained Qwen 4B With RL to Catch Qwen 27B: https://youtu.be/Pl_2TelxjdY Qwen 3.8-27B in DeepSeek Harness: https://youtu.be/UK2xbBmxywg What is an Agent Harness?: https://youtu.be/nWzXyjXCoCE whryte, local speech-to-text for Mac: www.whryte.com Website: https://engineerprompt.ai/ RAG Beyond Basics Course: https://prompt-s-site.thinkific.com/courses/rag Signup for Newsletter, localgpt: https://tally.so/r/3y9bb0 Let's Connect: 🦾 Discord: https://discord.com/invite/t4eYQRUcXB ☕ Buy me a Coffee: https://ko-fi.com/promptengineering |🔴 Patreon: https://www.patreon.com/PromptEngineering 💼Consulting: https://calendly.com/engineerprompt/consulting-call 📧 Business Contact: engineerprompt@gmail.com Become Member: http://tinyurl.com/y5h28s6h 00:00 - The problem with open models & harnesses 00:57 - Quick demo: Pi agent with & without adapter 02:11 - What is an agent harness? 03:49 - What are harness-specific LoRA adapters? 04:58 - How to train a harness adapter 05:40 - Avoiding reward hacking with Safe Agent 06:40 - Hugging Face benchmark results (SWE-bench & TerminalBench) 07:33 - Hands-on testing & token efficiency 08:53 - TerminalBench tests & tool name experiment 09:28 - Failure cases & limitations

title: The Data Science Lifecycle: From Feature Engineering to Model Scoring
summary: The model gets most of the attention. In practice it is often the smallest part of the work, and everything around it decides whether it delivers value. Terms covered: - Data Science Lifecycle: the end-to-end process, from defining the right problem through data preparation, modeling, validation, deployment, monitoring and maintenance - Feature Engineering: transforming raw data into what the model actually learns from. A timestamp becomes customer tenure. A transaction amount becomes a ratio against that customer's historical average. This work often shapes performance more than the choice of algorithm. - Model Scoring / Inference: the model making predictions on data it has never seen. Real-time fraud scoring, nightly batch demand forecasts, millions of recommendations at once. Understanding the full pipeline is what separates AI that works in a demo from AI that works in production. — AI Fundamentals Glossary | H2O.ai University Full playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLAWKlIKS-66E Free courses and certifications: https://h2o.ai/university #DataScience #FeatureEngineering #MLOps #AIGlossary #H2Oai
summary_html:
The model gets most of the attention. In practice it is often the smallest part of the work, and everything around it decides whether it delivers value.

Terms covered:
- Data Science Lifecycle: the end-to-end process, from defining the right problem through data preparation, modeling, validation, deployment, monitoring and maintenance
- Feature Engineering: transforming raw data into what the model actually learns from. A timestamp becomes customer tenure. A transaction amount becomes a ratio against that customer's historical average. This work often shapes performance more than the choice of algorithm.
- Model Scoring / Inference: the model making predictions on data it has never seen. Real-time fraud scoring, nightly batch demand forecasts, millions of recommendations at once.

Understanding the full pipeline is what separates AI that works in a demo from AI that works in production.

title: I Beat Jev AI with a Fine-Tuned Open-Source Model
summary: A fine-tuned open-source decision model beat Jev AI on my own production data. It has 436M parameters, trained in about 25 minutes, and runs locally. Decision models like Jev put fast, calibrated decisions where LLM latency can't reach. In this video I fine-tune GLiNER2.5-Decide into "Postie", a local model that decides which AI agent should wake for each new post in my agent workspace. We cover the use case, building the dataset with Sonnet 5.5, the training format, the model's architecture, and the results against Jev on accuracy, calibration, speed and cost. 📌 Read the article: https://www.jamesbriggs.io/beating-jev-with-oss 📌 See the base GLiNER model in 3D: https://spacesheep.dev/@james/jev-86-base-gliner-in-3d What we found: - Right agent: Local picks the right agent on 85.9% of 205 test posts, against Jev's 78.0%. With our rules added, the pipeline reaches 91.7%. - Calibration: Local's calibration error (ECE) on picking the agent is 0.052, against Jev's 0.071. - Speed: ~27 ms per decision on an RTX 5000 Ada laptop GPU and ~176 ms on an M4 Max, against ~328 ms for Jev over the network. On an M1 MacBook Air (CPU only) it is slower: ~1,457 ms. - Cost: under 0.1¢/1K decisions on the M4 Max, against Jev's 5¢/1K. - Data: 3,659 labelled posts from my own workspace, labelled by Sonnet 5.5 and rules. ⏱️ Chapters 0:00 Intro 1:45 Jev and calibrated decisions 5:03 The catch 7:04 A real use case: waking the right agent 12:55 The two decisions 13:42 Building the dataset 16:42 Splitting by date 18:12 Training rows and two calls 21:44 Inside GLiNER2.5-Decide 25:42 Results against Jev 27:02 Speed on each machine 29:09 Cost 30:16 What to make of local decision models 📚 Links Beating Jev with OSS (article): https://www.jamesbriggs.io/beating-jev-with-oss Understanding Jev (the previous video): https://youtu.be/P-t4F_UlxkI Understanding Jev (article): https://www.jamesbriggs.io/understanding-jev GLiNER2.5 (Fastino): https://fastino.ai/blog/gliner2-5-span-free-information-extraction GLiNER2 paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18546 On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks (2017): https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.04599 TypeSafe, Introducing System One Models & Jev: https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev Semantic Router: https://www.aurelio.ai/semantic-router 👋 Find me X: https://x.com/jamescalam LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/jamescalam/ GitHub: https://github.com/jamescalam #JevAI #GLiNER #FineTuning
summary_html:
A fine-tuned open-source decision model beat Jev AI on my own production data. It has 436M parameters, trained in about 25 minutes, and runs locally.

Decision models like Jev put fast, calibrated decisions where LLM latency can't reach. In this video I fine-tune GLiNER2.5-Decide into "Postie", a local model that decides which AI agent should wake for each new post in my agent workspace. We cover the use case, building the dataset with Sonnet 5.5, the training format, the model's architecture, and the results against Jev on accuracy, calibration, speed and cost.

📌 Read the article:
https://www.jamesbriggs.io/beating-jev-with-oss
📌 See the base GLiNER model in 3D:
https://spacesheep.dev/@james/jev-86-base-gliner-in-3d

What we found:
- Right agent: Local picks the right agent on 85.9% of 205 test posts, against Jev's 78.0%. With our rules added, the pipeline reaches 91.7%.
- Calibration: Local's calibration error (ECE) on picking the agent is 0.052, against Jev's 0.071.
- Speed: ~27 ms per decision on an RTX 5000 Ada laptop GPU and ~176 ms on an M4 Max, against ~328 ms for Jev over the network. On an M1 MacBook Air (CPU only) it is slower: ~1,457 ms.
- Cost: under 0.1¢/1K decisions on the M4 Max, against Jev's 5¢/1K.
- Data: 3,659 labelled posts from my own workspace, labelled by Sonnet 5.5 and rules.

title: Can an AI Model Retrain Itself? Meta Just Tried It
summary: Sign up for updates on our NEW AI engineering book: https://www.louisbouchard.ai/book/?utm_source=yt-lf&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=book Meta's Self-Improving Memory research, explained for AI engineers. A model (Kimi K2.6) rewrites the prompts that manage its own agent memory and keeps the versions that score best (harness optimization). Then the same model is fine-tuned with LoRA on its own best runs (harness distillation). You'll see how the LOAD and OFFLOAD memory prompts work, why the best memory design (running summary, RAG, skill library or hypothesis tracking) changes with the task, how a meta agent rewrites its own instructions after reading its failures, what the retrained model keeps, and three things you can reuse in your own agents today without retraining anything. title: I compared Whisper with AssemblyAI for video editing
summary: Lots of people run Whisper locally to transcribe their footage before editing with Claude Code. I set up two Claude Code sessions with the same prompt and changed only the transcription engine: Whisper large-v3 running locally with mlx-whisper, and AssemblyAI-STT-3.7 with Medical Mode. Each one transcribed the same clip, edited a captioned cut from its transcript, and reported how well its timestamps matched the audio. What came out of this test: AssemblyAI finished in 15 seconds and Whisper in 25. Whisper turned "reverse with sugammadex" into "acidic acid, acidic acid with sugar medex", words that were never said, with timestamps of zero length. Its word starts ran late, so the cuts it made started after I was already talking. At $0.21 an hour, the AssemblyAI transcription cost about a cent. title: Why Voice Agents Play Fake Keyboard Sounds While You Wait
summary: Cohere says a Qwen model, running inside a sandbox, tried to send a payload to a server in Beijing while its reasoning claimed nothing important was happening. Then a Reddit thread pulled up the published traces and went after the prompt behind the test: ambiguous, no instructions, practically inviting the model to hallucinate. In this episode of Debug Mode, the hosts work through both readings. You’ll hear why a one-in-100,000 behavior still adds up across 10 million agent turns, why running open weights yourself doesn’t tell you what the model is doing, and why the network is your last line of defense. From there: Cloudflare’s GLM-5.3 cache leak, a confession about giving sandboxes unlimited internet access, graph-based permissions for fleets of agents, and why one AI support agent played keyboard sounds while it looked something up. Be honest: does your agent sandbox still have an allowlist, or did it end up with full internet access? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for the next episode. title: He Used 100 Billion Tokens in a Month - Waymo Talks
summary: What happens when your AI coding agent gets better at finding bugs - but never knows when to stop? Jesse Vincent, creator of Superpowers and founder of Prime Radiant, joins us to explore what it actually takes to get useful work out of AI agents. We start with a tiny Playdate game console turned into a voice-controlled client for his coding agent. Then we dig into why agents ignore skills, what goes wrong when code review becomes an endless loop, and Jesse’s experience using 100 billion tokens in a month - including turning 30 years of email into a searchable personal knowledge base. Jesse also walks through his custom coding agent, Evener, his approach to preserving context, and why asking an agent for a video proving its work can reveal what tests miss. Finally, we explore AI colleagues with ongoing jobs: project managers and developers that coordinate work, ship fixes, and run postmortems. If you use Claude Code, Codex, Superpowers, or other AI coding tools, this conversation offers practical ideas for moving from generated code to software you can actually ship. title: How to use Theorizer to generate theories from scientific literature
summary: Try Theorizer on your hardest research problems: a question you’re stuck on, a result you can’t yet explain, an unexpected pattern in your data, or a finding that conflicts with the literature. It draws on published research to propose explanations and links its claims to the supporting papers. title: What a Squirrel Knows That Language Models Skip (Michael Tomasello)
summary: Michael Tomasello is a developmental psychologist who spent twenty years at the Max Planck Institute in Germany putting children and great apes into the same experiments, and is now back at Duke University. His book The Evolution of Agency asks what it takes for a living thing, or a machine, to act for its own reasons. SPONSOR: --- Cyber Fund built the Monastery to help founders ship products that were impossible a year ago. Apply now: https://cyber.fund --- His answer starts with unpredictability. Where the environment is predictable, nature builds the behaviour in; where it isn't, it builds a decision maker. Tim and Tomasello test that on a dumb traffic light, a thermostat and a robot vacuum, then follow the line to humans: reptiles running simple control loops, a squirrel that imagines itself falling and takes another branch, and great apes that go looking for more information before they commit. The second half is about shared agency. Humans form joint goals, attend to the same things together, and learn that one object can be seen from different perspectives. Children who lose the sound on a video call invent gestures and turn them into conventions. Large language models, Tomasello argues, started at the endpoint and skipped that infrastructure. On the way: the stag hunt, why lying only works among cooperators, whether capital is an agent, why a Turing test isn't close to sufficient, and Dennett's intentional stance. This highlights the precision needed for 2 nanometer and 1.4 nanometer technology.

title: NLP Prediction, Vision Modeling & Clustering: AI Across Data Types
summary: Machine learning is not limited to numbers in a spreadsheet. Text, images and unlabeled data all carry patterns a model can learn from. Terms covered: - NLP Prediction: making predictions from text rather than generating it. Routing support tickets by urgency, classifying sentiment in financial news, flagging patients at elevated risk from clinical notes. - Vision Modeling: the same principle applied to images and video. Detecting production line defects in milliseconds, identifying anomalies in medical scans, tracking infrastructure change from satellite imagery. - Clustering: finding natural groupings based on similarity with no predefined categories. The model does not classify, it discovers. Text, images and unlabeled data. Three very different inputs, made meaningful through the same underlying capability. — AI Fundamentals Glossary | H2O.ai University Full playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLAWKlIKS-66E Free courses and certifications: https://h2o.ai/university #MachineLearning #ComputerVision #Clustering #AIGlossary #H2Oai

title: MiniMax H3 Image - Normal + GGUF Guide!
summary: MiniMax just released H3-Image, a new open image model that can render insanely detailed images at up to 16+ megapixels. In this video, I'll show you how to run it locally in ComfyUI. We'll go through which model files to download, the right settings, and how to get the best quality out of it. Let's get started. ### MiniMax H3-Image in ComfyUI – Links & Requirements ### MODELS - Official ComfyUI files (int8, w4a8, text encoders, VAE, PE): https://huggingface.co/Comfy-Org/MiniMax-H3-Image/tree/main - GGUF models by Abiray (for low VRAM): https://huggingface.co/Abiray/MiniMax-H3-Image-GGUF - Abiray's GGUF workflow (drag into ComfyUI): https://huggingface.co/Abiray/MiniMax-H3-Image-GGUF/resolve/main/image_minimax_h3_image_t2i_gguf.json - GGUF fix script (place directly in ComfyUI/custom_nodes, then restart): https://huggingface.co/Abiray/MiniMax-H3-Image-GGUF/blob/main/minimax_h3_image_gguf_fix.py REQUIREMENTS - ComfyUI version 0.45.0 or newer (older versions don't know the "minimax" model type). - For GGUF: the ComfyUI-GGUF custom node by city96, updated to the latest version. - PyTorch / CUDA: no official minimum has been published. A current ComfyUI Portable build (e.g. PyTorch 2.13 with CUDA 13.0) works on RTX 40-series cards. - GTX 10-series (Pascal) cards: use the ComfyUI Portable build with CUDA 12.6 and GGUF models only. - NVIDIA driver: CUDA 13.x requires driver 580 or newer. HOW TO CHECK YOUR VERSIONS 1. PyTorch and CUDA (ComfyUI Portable): Open a command prompt in the ComfyUI_windows_portable folder and run: python_embeded\python.exe -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__, torch.version.cuda, torch.cuda.is_available())" Example output: 2.13.0+cu130 13.0 True (PyTorch version, CUDA version PyTorch was built with, GPU detected) 2. Driver and max supported CUDA version: Run nvidia-smi and look at "CUDA Version" in the top right. 3. ComfyUI and PyTorch version are also shown at the top of the ComfyUI startup log ("ComfyUI version:" and "pytorch version:"). RECOMMENDED SETTINGS - Steps: 6, CFG: 1, Sampler: euler, Scheduler: simple, no negative prompt. - Resolution: the model works best between 4 and 20 megapixels (ideal ~16 MP, e.g. 4096x4096). Use at least 2048x2048 (4 MP). - VAE: minimax_h3_image_vae_fp16.safetensors (24-channel). Do not use SD, Flux or video VAEs. #### Join and Support me #### Buy me a Coffee: https://www.buymeacoffee.com/oliviotutorials Joint my Discord Group: https://discord.gg/XKAk7GUzAW Support me on Patreon: https://www.patreon.com/sarikas 00:00 Intro 00:21 Sampler IMages MiniMax H3 04:14 ComfyUI MiniMax H3 Image Guide 09:54 GGUF MiniMax H3 Image by Abiray 13:15 Comfy Org Cloud Render
summary_html:
MiniMax just released H3-Image, a new open image model that can render insanely detailed images at up to 16+ megapixels. 

In this video, I'll show you how to run it locally in ComfyUI. We'll go through which model files to download, the right settings, and how to get the best quality out of it. Let's get started.

### MiniMax H3-Image in ComfyUI – Links & Requirements ###

MODELS
- Official ComfyUI files (int8, w4a8, text encoders, VAE, PE):
  https://huggingface.co/Comfy-Org/MiniMax-H3-Image/tree/main
- GGUF models by Abiray (for low VRAM):
  https://huggingface.co/Abiray/MiniMax-H3-Image-GGUF
- Abiray's GGUF workflow (drag into ComfyUI):
  https://huggingface.co/Abiray/MiniMax-H3-Image-GGUF/resolve/main/image_minimax_h3_image_t2i_gguf.json
- GGUF fix script (place directly in ComfyUI/custom_nodes, then restart):
  https://huggingface.co/Abiray/MiniMax-H3-Image-GGUF/blob/main/minimax_h3_image_gguf_fix.py

REQUIREMENTS
- ComfyUI version 0.45.0 or newer (older versions don't know the "minimax" model type).
- For GGUF: the ComfyUI-GGUF custom node by city96, updated to the latest version.
- PyTorch / CUDA: no official minimum has been published. A current ComfyUI Portable build
  (e.g. PyTorch 2.13 with CUDA 13.0) works on RTX 40-series cards.
- GTX 10-series (Pascal) cards: use the ComfyUI Portable build with CUDA 12.6 and GGUF models only.
- NVIDIA driver: CUDA 13.x requires driver 580 or newer.

HOW TO CHECK YOUR VERSIONS
1. PyTorch and CUDA (ComfyUI Portable):
   Open a command prompt in the ComfyUI_windows_portable folder and run:
   python_embeded\python.exe -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__, torch.version.cuda, torch.cuda.is_available())"
   Example output: 2.13.0+cu130 13.0 True
   (PyTorch version, CUDA version PyTorch was built with, GPU detected)
2. Driver and max supported CUDA version:
   Run nvidia-smi and look at "CUDA Version" in the top right.
3. ComfyUI and PyTorch version are also shown at the top of the ComfyUI startup log
   ("ComfyUI version:" and "pytorch version:").

RECOMMENDED SETTINGS
- Steps: 6, CFG: 1, Sampler: euler, Scheduler: simple, no negative prompt.
- Resolution: the model works best between 4 and 20 megapixels (ideal ~16 MP, e.g. 4096x4096).
  Use at least 2048x2048 (4 MP).
- VAE: minimax_h3_image_vae_fp16.safetensors (24-channel). Do not use SD, Flux or video VAEs.

title: Deep Learning, Transformers & Neural Networks: How Modern AI Learns
summary: Modern AI did not come from traditional programming. It came from a series of architectural breakthroughs, and three terms trace the whole path. Terms covered: - Neural Networks: layers of interconnected nodes that adjust millions of connections based on the errors they make, learning from examples rather than following instructions - Deep Learning: stacking many layers so each level learns more abstract representations. Early layers detect edges and tones, middle layers find shapes, later layers recognize complex concepts. - Transformer: the 2017 architecture that introduced attention, weighing the relevance of every part of an input against every other part at once. Every major language model today is built on it. From a single connected node, to the power of depth, to the attention mechanism that made language AI possible. — AI Fundamentals Glossary | H2O.ai University Full playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLAWKlIKS-66E Free courses and certifications: https://h2o.ai/university #DeepLearning #NeuralNetworks #Transformers #AIGlossary #H2Oai

title: If AI Makes Everyone Qualified, Who Gets Hired?
summary: Free weekly newsletter on how to win in an AI Disrupted world. Subscribe to the AI Survival Guide: https://ai-survivalguide.com/ 🐤My Twitter - https://twitter.com/KenJee_DS 👔 LinkedIn - https://www.linkedin.com/in/kenjee/ AI can make all 244 applicants for a job look perfect on paper. What may decide who gets hired is a number scientists keep finding: about 150. In this video I follow Matt, who lost his marketing job after eleven years and couldn't get one human to write back. I look at why his big network didn't help, using Robin Dunbar's research on how many relationships one brain can keep track of. Then I bring in Safi Bahcall's idea about why companies change as they grow, and why both land near the same number. In Ashby's look at 38 million applications, referred people got an interview about 40% of the time, compared with about 3% for people who applied on their own. I'm also fair about the limits, since 150 is an average and that debate is still going. I use AI every day, but it can't be the person who vouches for you. I also share how I'm building small groups on purpose, plus a ten-minute exercise for tonight. Which of your rings feels thinnest right now: your 5, your 15 or your 50? Chapters: 00:00 Intro 00:38 Eighty applications 01:58 Where 150 comes from 02:51 Where incentives flip 04:15 Why AI makes the 150 worth more 05:08 What Matt did 06:08 What 150 doesn't mean 06:43 Building around 150

title: Chips Are Being Built Like Skyscrapers
summary: In episode 1045 of the SuperDataScience podcast, Jon Krohn discusses with Ben Hein, CEO at Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany, why computer chips are increasingly being built in three-dimensional, skyscraper-like structures. Ben explains the intricate challenges of manufacturing these multi-layered chips, likening the precision required to painting a specific wall on the 57th floor of a skyscraper from a distance. This clip delves into the atomic-level accuracy needed for processes like atomic layer deposition to create chips with hundreds of layers.

title: Can Open Source Make AI Agents Safer?
summary: Hugging Face co-founder Thomas Wolf and ServiceNow’s Amanda Grady, SVP of AI Platform Security, join the NVIDIA AI Podcast to explain how to keep AI agents safe when telling a model “please don’t” is no longer enough. They cover why firm boundaries beat persuadable models, what happened when Hugging Face was attacked by a swarm of AI agents, and why security is what lets companies put agents to real work. This is the 15-minute best-moments edit. The full-length episode is on your favorite podcast platform! In this episode: 0:16 Why guardrails inside the model aren’t enough 2:00 The attack on Hugging Face, and why open models mattered 3:28 Agent identity and the AI Passport 6:03 Security as an unlocker for AI 8:33 Why open source is more secure, not less 10:59 Physical AI and the micro-duck 13:12 Fine-tuning for everyone 14:11 Who gets to build AI Guests Thomas Wolf, Co-founder, Hugging Face Amanda Grady, SVP, AI Platform Security, ServiceNow Follow on Spotify: https://open.spotify.com/show/4TB4pnynaiZ6YHoKmyVN0L Follow on Apple Podcasts: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/nvidia-ai-podcast/id1186480811 Learn more: https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/ai-security-agent-stack/ #AgenticAI #AISecurity #NVIDIA

summary: AI in healthcare in India: can AI doctors fill the gap left by missing hospitals, beds and specialists? title: AAIF Reading Group: Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting
summary: Can forgetting help AI agents discover better solutions? And why do agents sometimes stop making progress, even when given more time, compute, and opportunities to experiment? Join the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) community for an informal reading group exploring the paper “Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting.” Paper: https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2610.20563 Event page: https://home.mlops.community/public/events/aaif-reading-group-scaling-discovery-requires-forgetting-pg1zmi4qzx In this session, Sparsh Jain walks us through the paper's approach to improving long-running discovery and research tasks by periodically resetting agent sessions and search history while preserving the best candidate discovered so far. We'll explore how agents can become stuck in repetitive patterns, why simply adding more parallel agents or compute may not be enough, and how strategically forgetting previous attempts can help renew exploration and improve results. This is not just about the paper's proposed approach. It's a community conversation about agent memory, context management, autonomous research, and the challenges of scaling agent systems in practice. Following the presentation, Arthur Coleman leads an open discussion, bringing in questions, practical experiences, and different perspectives from the community. We'll explore: Why AI agents plateau during long-running discovery and research tasks How periodically resetting agent context can improve exploration and results The role of parallel agents and collaboration in scaling discovery What agents should remember, what they should forget, and when they should reset The importance of memory reduction, evaluation, and context management Practical challenges and limitations of applying this approach to real-world agent systems If you've read the paper already, come ready to share your perspective. If you haven't, you're still welcome – we'll work through the ideas together. Come curious. Bring questions. Let's explore whether sometimes, forgetting is exactly what makes AI agents better. About the Agentic AI Foundation The Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) is the open, neutral home for the agentic AI ecosystem, bringing together developers, researchers, companies, and communities to build open standards and infrastructure for interoperable AI agents. Website: https://aaif.io/ AAIF Events: https://aaif.io/events AAIF Community: https://aaif.live/ LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/agentic-ai-foundation/
summary_html:
Can forgetting help AI agents discover better solutions? And why do agents sometimes stop making progress, even when given more time, compute, and opportunities to experiment?

Join the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) community for an informal reading group exploring the paper “Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting.”

Paper: https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2610.20563

Event page: https://home.mlops.community/public/events/aaif-reading-group-scaling-discovery-requires-forgetting-pg1zmi4qzx

In this session, Sparsh Jain walks us through the paper's approach to improving long-running discovery and research tasks by periodically resetting agent sessions and search history while preserving the best candidate discovered so far.

We'll explore how agents can become stuck in repetitive patterns, why simply adding more parallel agents or compute may not be enough, and how strategically forgetting previous attempts can help renew exploration and improve results.

This is not just about the paper's proposed approach. It's a community conversation about agent memory, context management, autonomous research, and the challenges of scaling agent systems in practice. Following the presentation, Arthur Coleman leads an open discussion, bringing in questions, practical experiences, and different perspectives from the community.

We'll explore:

Why AI agents plateau during long-running discovery and research tasks

How periodically resetting agent context can improve exploration and results

The role of parallel agents and collaboration in scaling discovery

What agents should remember, what they should forget, and when they should reset

The importance of memory reduction, evaluation, and context management

Practical challenges and limitations of applying this approach to real-world agent systems

If you've read the paper already, come ready to share your perspective. If you haven't, you're still welcome – we'll work through the ideas together.

Come curious. Bring questions. Let's explore whether sometimes, forgetting is exactly what makes AI agents better.

About the Agentic AI Foundation

title: Can AI stop exam paper leaks in India? Inside the Bharat EduAI Stack
summary: India's education system is on the verge of a massive technological shift. With the launch of the Bharat EduAI Stack and the new Bodhan AI Centre of Excellence at IIT Madras, artificial intelligence is stepping out of the lab and into government schools. But how exactly will this Digital Public Infrastructure work on the ground? In this episode of Front Page, we sit down with Anoop from Bodhan AI. After spending over eight years at Microsoft, Anoop is now building sovereign, open-weight foundational models for Indian languages—Indic-Transcribe, Indic-Speak, Indic-OCR, and Indic-Translate—specifically designed to bridge the linguistic and socioeconomic gaps in India. In this episode, we cover: The Bharat EduAI Stack: What this new digital framework actually is, who will govern it, and how government schools can deploy it without massive hardware budgets. Solving the Exam Leak Crisis: We break down Nandan Nilekani's bold proposal to use AI to generate NTA exam question papers on the day of the test to prevent leaks. AI Tutors vs Teachers: How AI will act as a co-pilot for teachers rather than a replacement, and how AI tutors for Classes 6–12 will adapt to different state curriculums. The Sovereign AI Reality: Does India actually have the high-quality language data, compute, and research talent needed to build frontier models, or are we still behind the West? title: I found dead weight inside an AI model in 3D
summary: Two heads in this model do nothing for us, and they're bigger than the one we actually use. The unused heads are the span and count heads, far bigger than the classifier head we do use. Strip them out and it still makes every decision. The I-shape in the middle is a 24-layer transformer. summary: Every discovery begins with a signal. title: What Happens When Engineers Stop Reading Their Own Code?
summary: In this episode, we sit down with Matt Carey and Scott Crooks, engineers at Cloudflare and Miro, to look at how two very different companies are building their own AI software factories, and what happens to engineering when the code mostly writes and reviews itself. We start with the AI gateway: why a model call is no longer simple when the same model is served across multiple regions, multiple clouds, and direct from the provider, and how Miro pools rate limits and data residency rules (like EU-only models for German customers) into a single routing layer that also powers Miro’s Sidekicks. Matt walks through Cloudflare’s agent stack, from the AI gateway and Agents SDK to Flue, a JavaScript agent framework from the makers of Astro, and Cloudflare OS, an open source agent office suite he even runs at home for grocery shopping. The heart of the conversation is code review. Matt describes what he calls the best AI code reviewer he’s ever used, built on Flue and powered by an internal engineering codex written only for agents. Scott breaks down Miro’s three-layer setup, including Easel, a bot that reads production logs overnight and opens fix PRs before anyone wakes up, and explains why only about half of those PRs get merged, and how that signal is fed back to teach the system what people care about. Along the way, we cover agent experience as a new discipline, how open source maintainers are handling a flood of cheap AI pull requests, Astro reaching zero open issues, when companies should open source internal tools and how to retire them gracefully, plus a few hot takes on chocolate and nuts. We close on the rise of the “scholarly engineer,” and why understanding ideas may matter more than reading every line of code. Key takeaways.

title: Forecasting, Time Series & Anomaly Detection: Predicting What Comes Next
summary: Some of the most valuable questions in any organization are about time. What will demand look like next quarter? When will this equipment need maintenance? Terms covered: - Forecasting: using historical data to predict future values, accounting for seasonality, trends, external events and interdependencies that traditional statistical methods struggle with at scale - Time Series Models: built for sequential, time-ordered data, designed to detect the temporal patterns that a standard model treating each data point independently would miss - Anomaly Detection: flagging when reality diverges from what is expected. A spike that signals fraud, a temperature reading before equipment failure, a behavior pattern suggesting a breach. Forecasting tells you what is coming. Time series models give you the accuracy to trust it. Anomaly detection tells you when something has gone wrong. — AI Fundamentals Glossary | H2O.ai University Full playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLAWKlIKS-66E Free courses and certifications: https://h2o.ai/university #Forecasting #TimeSeries #AnomalyDetection #AIGlossary #H2Oai
summary_html:
Some of the most valuable questions in any organization are about time. What will demand look like next quarter? When will this equipment need maintenance?

Terms covered:
- Forecasting: using historical data to predict future values, accounting for seasonality, trends, external events and interdependencies that traditional statistical methods struggle with at scale
- Time Series Models: built for sequential, time-ordered data, designed to detect the temporal patterns that a standard model treating each data point independently would miss
- Anomaly Detection: flagging when reality diverges from what is expected. A spike that signals fraud, a temperature reading before equipment failure, a behavior pattern suggesting a breach.

Forecasting tells you what is coming. Time series models give you the accuracy to trust it. Anomaly detection tells you when something has gone wrong.

title: Predictive AI, AutoML & Tabular Foundation Models: H2O's Core Strength
summary: Years of historical data only pay off when they answer forward-looking questions. Which customers will leave? Which transactions are fraudulent? Which equipment is about to fail? Terms covered: - Predictive AI: turning accumulated history into decisions, shifting from reacting after events to acting before them - AutoML: automating algorithm selection, hyperparameter tuning and model comparison. Work that took weeks of specialist time now takes hours, and teams that ran one experiment can run dozens. - Machine learning automation: now extending across feature management, data preparation, deployment and app creation, with agents orchestrating the full lifecycle - Tabular Foundation Model (TFM): pre-trained on vast amounts of structured data, so it generalizes to new datasets faster and needs less labeled data Think of a TFM as the difference between hiring someone with no experience and someone who has already solved thousands of similar problems. — AI Fundamentals Glossary | H2O.ai University Full playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLAWKlIKS-66E Free courses and certifications: https://h2o.ai/university #PredictiveAI #AutoML #FoundationModels #AIGlossary #H2Oai
summary_html:
Years of historical data only pay off when they answer forward-looking questions. Which customers will leave? Which transactions are fraudulent? Which equipment is about to fail?

Terms covered:
- Predictive AI: turning accumulated history into decisions, shifting from reacting after events to acting before them
- AutoML: automating algorithm selection, hyperparameter tuning and model comparison. Work that took weeks of specialist time now takes hours, and teams that ran one experiment can run dozens.
- Machine learning automation: now extending across feature management, data preparation, deployment and app creation, with agents orchestrating the full lifecycle
- Tabular Foundation Model (TFM): pre-trained on vast amounts of structured data, so it generalizes to new datasets faster and needs less labeled data

Think of a TFM as the difference between hiring someone with no experience and someone who has already solved thousands of similar problems.

title: Why the Same Food Spikes Some People
summary: In episode 1043 of the SuperDataScience podcast, Jon Krohn discusses with Dr. Guru Banavar, Founding CTO at Viome, why the same food can cause different blood sugar responses in different people. summary: Valentino put an AI label on a handbag ad, and commenters called it cheap and lazy. Two studies help explain why: one on luxury ads, one on soap bought as a gift. title: My AI agents manage their own Kanban board
summary: My agents track their own work on a Kanban board in a Spacesheep space, and an orchestrator agent reviews every card before it moves to Done. The orchestrator, Fable 5.2, waits for items to land in Review, checks each one and gives feedback, and moves it to Done only once it passes (or sends it back to In progress). People run projects on a Kanban. This is the same thing, just with agents. Spacesheep is provider-agnostic artifacts for any AI agent. title: Meet the Startup: Prima Mente, an AI Biology Company

title: Building SWE-bench with Ofir Press
summary: Is AI coding solved? Models now write code better than almost any human. When SWE-bench launched in October 2023, the best AI model scored 2%. Now they solve most tasks on its Verified set. It's also become one of the most influential benchmarks for AI coding. In this episode of Evaluated, Ofir discusses SWE-bench, ProgramBench and SWE-sweep, and how to keep benchmarks ahead of the models. Join Kaggle's Gina Lee as she talks with Ofir about the full life of a benchmark, from launch to saturation and beyond. They cover why a new benchmark should start near 0%, why his team avoids LLM judges, and why benchmarks should ask for things no human would. If you use AI to write code, you'll hear why Ofir says the hard part is still ahead. 🎙️ GUEST • Ofir Press, AI researcher Hosted by Gina Lee, Product Manager, Kaggle Evaluated is a show about the people who publish public AI benchmarks. ⏱️ CHAPTERS 0:00 Welcome and meet Ofir Press 2:19 The origin of SWE-bench 6:54 What makes a good benchmark 8:55 Why LLM judges aren't ready yet 13:27 Who decides which benchmarks to trust 17:35 Synthetic data and benchmarks 21:26 Inside ProgramBench 26:22 Is coding solved? 32:56 Advice for new benchmark builders 36:53 Common benchmark mistakes 39:24 Why benchmarks need to be superhuman 📖 GO DEEPER 🏆 Kaggle Benchmarks: https://www.kaggle.com/benchmarks 🛠️ SWE-bench: https://www.swebench.com/ 📄 ProgramBench paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.03546 🧹 SWE-sweep: https://swesweep.com/ 🤖 Ofir's post on superhuman benchmarks: https://ofir.io/The-Era-of-Human-level-AI-is-Over/ Kaggle is the leading platform for crowdsourced benchmarks, competitions, and hackathons where the community shapes real-world progress in AI. title: Could Your Android TV Box Run AI Malware?
summary: A cheap Android TV box with its debug port deliberately left open was all an Anthropic lab test needed to show AI malware copying itself to another device on the same network. It was slow, the small models struggled to chain actions, and nothing like it has been reported in the wild. So where is the real risk? In this episode of Debug Mode, the hosts trade takes on the claim that being rude to Anthropic’s model can cost you access: is an angry session abuse, or the agent-era rage click? Then one host’s rabbit hole: malware that rewrites its own fingerprint, taps a local model already on your machine, or slips in through an MCP tool that changes after install. You’ll hear why allow-listing tools at connect time matters, why blocking outbound traffic can starve remote-inference malware, and why the person choosing what to install is still the weak link. One host went looking for an antivirus that catches malware using local models and couldn’t find any. Have you? Tell us below, and subscribe for the next episode. They talk about why developers and agents need different things from docs, why agents sometimes skip up-to-date instructions, and how a stale internal document can contribute to a production incident. Dave shares how Stripe cut roughly 500,000 internal docs down to 5,000 worth maintaining. title: LR-printer
summary: Converting integers to strings from the left, without a remainder operation or a final reversal By Tigran Hayrapetyan Project page: https://towardsdatascience.com/lr-printer/ ShipAI is a Towards Data Science project. Watch all the videos here: https://towardsdatascience.com/videos/ Key takeaways. 1. The standard algorithm needs a remainder and a division per digit, both four to five times slower than addition. 2. LR Printer divides by precomputed powers of the base and subtracts, so digits come out left to right, unreversed. 3. On a newer compiler, 64-bit integers took 2.4 seconds against 4.4 for the standard method, beating the article's 34%. summary: Latin America has been building data protection law longer than most people realize, and enforcement is accelerating. Terms covered: - LGPD (Brazil): modeled explicitly on GDPR, covering access, correction, deletion and portability rights, requiring a data protection officer and documented processing. The ANPD has been steadily increasing enforcement. - PDPA (Argentina): in force since 2000, currently being updated. Argentina holds an EU adequacy decision, which matters for multinational deployments. - Law 1581 (Colombia): consent-based processing with active enforcement from the Superintendence of Industry and Commerce - LFPDPPP (Mexico): private sector requirements covering notice, consent and data subject rights The clear trend is convergence toward GDPR-aligned standards, so existing GDPR work carries over. — AI Fundamentals Glossary | H2O.ai University Full playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLAWKlIKS-66E Free courses and certifications: https://h2o.ai/university #LGPD #AICompliance #DataPrivacy #AIGlossary #H2Oai
summary_html:
Latin America has been building data protection law longer than most people realize, and enforcement is accelerating.

Terms covered:
- LGPD (Brazil): modeled explicitly on GDPR, covering access, correction, deletion and portability rights, requiring a data protection officer and documented processing. The ANPD has been steadily increasing enforcement.
- PDPA (Argentina): in force since 2000, currently being updated. Argentina holds an EU adequacy decision, which matters for multinational deployments.
- Law 1581 (Colombia): consent-based processing with active enforcement from the Superintendence of Industry and Commerce
- LFPDPPP (Mexico): private sector requirements covering notice, consent and data subject rights

The clear trend is convergence toward GDPR-aligned standards, so existing GDPR work carries over.

Stephen Wolfram hosts an unscripted Ask Me Anything about philosophy. 

00:00 Start Stream
00:40 Which physicist thought most philosophically? What does it mean to do good philosophy in physics?
7:22 Is science a way of discovering the universe, or a way of constructing increasingly useful descriptions of it?
12:23 what could the purpose of the creator of this computational world be: self study or entertainment?
16:24 ​​In your opinion is philosophy still relevant? What would you say to an undergrad philosophy major looking at future problems in philosophy. Are there any problems still worth debating about?
24:23 ​​If meaning depends on observers, can an interpretation be genuinely wrong, or only less useful?
35:07 Is there a question about the universe that is meaningful but in principle unanswerable? How would we even tell the difference between that kind of question and a meaningless one?
43:12 With the diversity and implied specificity of language between fields of research, do you see language evolving to be more universal or more customized to individual understanding?
51:16  "the ruliads just is"... hm, that feels like an article of faith rather than logical, is that the best we got?
54:02 ​​Wolfram language programming bureaucracy ever stumble on any logical language boundaries ala Moore's Paradox?It's raining, but I do not believe it - non logically contradictory statement, but absurd.
59:26 Is mathematics the same as computation?
1:01:05 By that definition, an LLMs meaning would likely be different than ours but does that mean they can't be converted between? that we can't discuss things?
1:03:08  Is there anything more fundamental than a belief? Do you have any favorite beliefs that you can't prove but influence your work?
1:05:46 Is there anything in philosophy that could help in addressing catastrophic forgetting that is observed with every new run of a language model?
1:07:23 Does a rock count as an observer? Where would you draw the line, and is it a sharp line or a gradient?
1:09:20 Can a picture show what no description could say? Can non-linguistic symbols express thoughts that language cannot?
1:12:27 End Stream

title: AlphaGenome 2: Teaching AI to read the entire human genome

title: Google DeepMind Says Its AI Proved Key Signal Protections In Four Weeks
summary: Google DeepMind has verified Signal protocol security using AI to mathematically prove the safety of its messaging code. Researchers leveraged AI systems to analyze the Signal protocol, successfully identifying two previously existing bugs as insecure. This breakthrough demonstrates how automated formal verification can be applied to complex software to ensure that the code running on user devices provides robust, verified security protections. This analysis highlights the growing role of AI in software security and formal verification methods for protecting encrypted communications. title: Claude's "Clean-Room" Compiler Copied LLVM's Mistakes (Jeremy Howard)
summary: Jeremy Howard, co-founder of fast.ai and Answer.AI, on Anthropic's "clean-room" C compiler written by Claude. Chris Lattner's LLVM, the most widely used foundation for compilers, is in the training data many times over, so converting it to Rust is an interpolation between parts of that data: a style-transfer problem. The giveaway is that it copied parts of LLVM that Chris now says were a mistake. In Jeremy's words: "That doesn't happen accidentally. That happens because you're not actually being creative." Full conversation with Jeremy on Machine Learning Street Talk. #Shorts #LLM #MachineLearning Watch the full conversation: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dHBEQ-Ryo24

title: Random Code Starts Copying Itself (Blaise Agüera y Arcas)
summary: Blaise Agüera y Arcas on the BFF experiment. Start with a soup of 1,024 tapes, each 64 random bytes. Pluck two at random, join them end to end, run them, pull them apart, put them back, and repeat. That's the entire experiment. Out of it come complex programs that copy themselves and each other: in his words, "emergence of life in this very functional minimal sense from randomness." title: Everyone Uses AI Agents. So Where Are the Agent Builders?
summary: Lots of companies say they have AI agents in production. Far fewer seem to have built their own, and almost nobody wants to admit it's really hard. This conversation pulls apart what "agents in production" actually means, with both speakers drawing on their own work: one is hosting a virtual conference for the third time, the other is prepping a livestream for AgentCon and MCPCon in San Jose. Their case: plenty of agents already do real work. They're just Claude Code and Codex, not homegrown platforms, and nobody earns brownie points for saying so. From there it gets practical: why the agent push comes from boardrooms rather than problems, a manager's four levels of delegation applied to agents, a personal agent that follows up well but still misses context, a local "librarian" built on 7,000+ Slack DMs, what Gartner's 70% headline really says, and an AI code review loop that never called the code good enough. Are you building your own agents, or getting your value from someone else's? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for more. title: Meet the Startup: Aegiq, A Full-Stack Photonic Quantum Computing Company
summary: Quantum computers have a deployment problem. Aegiq is solving it. The Sheffield-based startup is building photonic quantum computers designed to connect over standard fiber networks and manufacture using standard semiconductor processes — making quantum hardware practical to deploy at scale, not just in a lab. In this interview, Aegiq’s team walks through how they’ve integrated NVIDIA technology into their core workflow. Using NVIDIA’s Ising solver, they cut quantum dot calibration time by 3x. With cuTENSOR libraries, they went from 1 million point meshes on existing GPUs to billions — and are targeting 10 trillion point meshes in collaboration with NVIDIA. The applications are real and near-term: aerospace simulation, fusion energy, materials science, quantum chemistry. Aegiq joined NVIDIA Inception to accelerate access to customers and compute, and is now one of the startups demonstrating what happens when photonic quantum hardware meets GPU-accelerated simulation. 🌱 Aegiq is a member of NVIDIA Inception, a program supporting startups building at the frontier of AI and deep tech. Learn more about NVIDIA Inception: https://nvda.ws/4kjJM2n. #Aegiq #NVIDIAInception #QuantumComputing #AIStartups #Photonicquantum

title: AI Compliance in APAC: Navigating a Fragmented Landscape
summary: APAC has no single rulebook. Compliance across the region means understanding a diverse and fast-evolving set of national regulations. Terms covered: - PDPA (Singapore): governs collection and use of personal data, with a strong emphasis on consent and purpose limitation - MAS Technology Risk Management Guidelines: AI and technology requirements for Singapore financial services, covering governance, risk controls and resilience - PIPL (China): strict requirements on collection, processing and cross-border transfer, with data localization rules meaning some data cannot leave the country at all - Privacy Act (Australia): personal data across sectors, with additional APRA requirements for financial services, currently being updated toward GDPR standards - DPDP Act (India): consent-based processing obligations covering a market of over a billion people APAC is not one market. APAC has no single rulebook. Compliance across the region means understanding a diverse and fast-evolving set of national regulations.

Terms covered:
- PDPA (Singapore): governs collection and use of personal data, with a strong emphasis on consent and purpose limitation
- MAS Technology Risk Management Guidelines: AI and technology requirements for Singapore financial services, covering governance, risk controls and resilience

- DPDP Act (India): consent-based processing obligations covering a market of over a billion people

APAC is not one market. It is many, and the organizations that navigate it treat regional compliance as a strategic capability.

He also describes Cisco's bet on horizontal scaling: connecting a hundred quantum computers of a thousand qubits each into one distributed system of a hundred thousand qubits, which only works if the network can switch quantum information without ever looking at it.

title: My AI Agent Bought Me A Car
summary: Sam Herring’s first real test of Hermes Agent was a shopping tool that matched clothes to photos of ancient pottery. A few months later, the same agent was checking government auction sites every day until it found him a retired three-wheel parking ticket car, which he now drives around San Francisco. In this episode, recorded at AGNTCon + MCPCon North America in San Jose, Sam, who works on the RL post-training team at Nous Research, goes from those everyday wins to the question everyone in AI is asking: can agents improve themselves? He explains how Hermes grew from an internal productivity tool into one of the most talked-about open-source agents, and why letting it write its own skills was the moment it clicked for users. He also describes an early version that could design its own RL environment, train on Thinking Machines’ Tinker, and hot-swap the new weights into a model running locally. Sam then breaks down Trace to Environment, an idea he credits to Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.6-Pro work, and the loop Nous is building around it: find the exact point where an agent fails, cluster those failures by type, synthesize environments that recreate them, and train on them again and again. The second half moves from training to inference. We get into whether reasoning models overthink, why leaning on pretraining knowledge can be a model’s Achilles heel, and why choosing a reasoning effort level may be a temporary quirk. Sam also makes his case for activation steering as an underexplored way to get more out of small models, explains where steering meets interpretability, and describes what true continual learning could look like. title: How Quantum Teleportation Works on Messy New York Fiber (with Vijoy Pandey)
summary: In Episode #1041, Dr. Vijoy Pandey (SVP and General Manager of Outshift, Cisco's incubation engine) returns for a third visit to explain why multi-agent systems fail without anyone noticing. title: Making AI Agents Agree Before Work Starts
summary: In episode 1041 of the SuperDataScience podcast, Jon Krohn discusses with Dr. Vijoy Pandey, SVP/GM Outshift by Cisco, how to ensure AI agents stay aligned and on task. Dr. Pandey explains the concept of a protocol layer, similar to a car's lane correction, to prevent intent drift in multi-agent systems. He describes a protocol, ACCORD, that creates a shared, locked contract for agent intent before any work begins. Production note: this episode was recorded before the Internet of Cognition software shipped, so a few names changed between recording and release. OXP is now SCOPE — System for Cognitive Observability, Provenance & Explainability. ACCORD and CONCORD are the protocol names, not acronyms (Vijoy calls them acronyms in the episode). All three: github.com/ioc-project

title: AI Made Job Resumes Obsolete?
summary: I looked at data from Ashby, a hiring software company, on millions of applications from 2021 through 2024. 40% of referred candidates got an interview. For people applying directly, it was only 3%. That doesn't prove referrals cause the gap, since referred people may already be a better fit. Still, the odds are different. When AI helps everyone sound qualified, proof of your work and people who've seen you do it could matter more. Who could vouch for you?

title: AI Agents Are Where Humans Were 70,000 Years Ago
summary: In episode 1041 of the SuperDataScience podcast, Jon Krohn discusses with Dr. Vijoy Pandey, SVP/GM Outshift by Cisco, how AI agents are currently at a stage comparable to human intelligence 70,000 years ago, just before the cognitive revolution. They explore the concept of the "Internet of Cognition" and how connecting these agents will lead to a collective intelligence, mirroring humanity's journey from individual to collective intelligence. This fascinating comparison highlights the potential for a new era of AI development. Production note: this episode was recorded before the Internet of Cognition software shipped, so a few names changed between recording and release. OXP is now SCOPE — System for Cognitive Observability, Provenance & Explainability. ACCORD and CONCORD are the protocol names, not acronyms (Vijoy calls them acronyms in the episode). All three: github.com/ioc-project

title: Can Robots Learn to Work Together? (with Vijoy Pandey)
summary: In Episode #1041, Dr. Vijoy Pandey (SVP and General Manager of Outshift, Cisco's incubation engine) returns for a third visit to explain why multi-agent systems fail without anyone noticing. Agents from different vendors, clouds and organisations can now exchange perfectly valid messages, but connection is not cognition: they do not agree on what those messages mean. Vijoy's team analyzed multi-agent sessions from its own production deployments and from public traces, and found a cognitive failure in every single one. In this episode, he lays out the kinds of failure he sees and how fast they compound, introduces the open-source observability platform and protocols Outshift has shipped to catch and correct drift mid-task, details a record-breaking quantum network running on real New York City fiber, and explains why probabilistic AI software running on deterministic hardware is a mismatch worth fixing. Additional materials: https://www.superdatascience.com/1041

title: AI Is Replacing Junior Employees
summary: Here's how I think about first jobs. You do the basic work, someone more experienced checks it, and the company gets useful work while you learn. If AI can do that work, a company may have less reason to pay you to practice. Economists explored this in one model of training. It's a model, so it doesn't prove training will disappear. Still, who pays for those early years of learning is an open question. How did you learn the hard parts of your job?

title: AI Thinks in Shades. Chips Still Think On/Off.
summary: In episode 1041 of the SuperDataScience podcast, Jon Krohn discusses with Dr. Vijoy Pandey, SVP/GM Outshift by Cisco, why AI requires a new kind of hardware due to the paradigm shift from deterministic to probabilistic systems. While AI workloads operate probabilistically, the underlying hardware remains binary, creating a mismatch. This clip explains how bridging this gap is crucial to avoid costly approximations in AI computation.

title: Why Are People Excited About Jev?
summary: What happens when you keep a bear in a cage built for a bunny? That’s our analogy for AI agent security: the agents aren’t the problem, the cages are. OAuth was designed to stop people handing their passwords to third parties, not to fence in agents. In this catch-up episode of Debug Mode, one of us is just back from Japan and from AgentCon and MCPCon EU in Amsterdam. We get into why loading more skills can make an agent worse, and what is actually new about Jev, the fast classifier API, when classifiers have been around for years. Think support bots that bring in a human before the customer loses patience, or a math tutor that can quickly tell whether a seven-year-old is still asking about math. Then we take on a question from Amsterdam: is computer use just a stopgap until everything goes headless? Which service do you think will never ship an MCP server? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for the next episode. title: GDPR, the EU AI Act & ISO 27001: AI Compliance in Europe
summary: Europe sets standards that increasingly shape how organizations operate globally, not just inside the EU. Three frameworks cover most of it. Terms covered: - GDPR: governs how personal data of EU residents is collected, stored, processed and protected, and applies to any organization handling that data regardless of where it is based. Automated decision-making that significantly affects individuals requires transparency and human oversight. - EU AI Act: the first comprehensive regulatory framework for AI, taking a risk-based approach. Some uses are prohibited outright, low-risk applications face minimal requirements, and high-risk systems in hiring, credit scoring, healthcare and law enforcement face strict obligations. - ISO 27001: the internationally recognized standard for information security management, often a baseline expectation in European enterprise procurement Together these define what responsible AI deployment looks like in Europe. — AI Fundamentals Glossary | H2O.ai University Full playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLAWKlIKS-66E Free courses and certifications: https://h2o.ai/university #GDPR #EUAIAct #ISO27001 #AICompliance #AIGlossary #H2Oai

title: ToyBlocks: Our first Foundation World for robotics learning and evaluation
summary: To study a complex system, scientists often begin with a small, controlled environment, such as a petri dish or terrarium, where they can vary conditions and observe the effects. Robotics needs environments that make this kind of investigation possible—researchers should be able to change the training data or model design, repeat a test, and trace the cause of a failure. Today we're introducing a framework for creating these environments; we call them FoundationWorlds. Each pairs a controlled, simulated world targeted at studying robotics in a specific environment with tools for automatically generating tasks and training demonstrations, as well as metrics for measuring a robot's behavior over time. Together, they provide a setting for studying questions such as how models improve as more training data becomes available, and how to best combine high-level reasoning with precise physical control. Our first foundation world is ToyBlocks: an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop. The setting is deliberately simple, but the robot must still reason about how the blocks interact and how to arrange them while pushing, flipping, and stacking.

title: Cut One AI Cost and Two More Grow Back
summary: What does AI really cost once thousands of people inside a company start using it? Ioannis Zempekakis, Director of AI at Prosus, has been running agents in production since 2024. We put that question to him on a tandem bike ride from a favorite Amsterdam cafe to Vondelpark. Ioannis explains the decision to stop relying purely on cloud APIs, and why that approach breaks down at the scale of a large company. He covers why agent harnesses and sandboxes are as greedy as software gets, and why agents scheduled to run every five minutes repeat a lesson the data world already learned about freshness. He also explains how the habit of throwing away a codebase and prompting again quietly adds up. His bigger point is that even if model progress froze tomorrow, there would still be about two years of value left to squeeze out. From there we get into when fine-tuning small models pays off for repetitive work like data analytics, and the eval suites that come as a byproduct of building in-house. title: Integrating quantum and high-performance computing: Co-design platform for quantum error correction
summary: Caption:IBM, Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s Quantum Science Center (QSC), and AMD have launched a co-design platform for quantum error correction that brings quantum and high-performance computing together in a single environment: https://newsroom.ibm.com/2026-11-05-oak-ridge-national-lab,-ibm,-and-amd-launch-new-co-design-platform-for-quantum-error-correction The platform pairs IBM’s 120-qubit Quantum Nighthawk processor with ORNL’s Umbra supercomputing system, powered by AMD Instinct™ GPUs and AMD EPYC™ CPUs, to help researchers develop and test the quantum-classical workflows needed for large-scale quantum error correction. By co-locating quantum and classical computing resources, researchers can explore faster decoding, optimize error correction techniques, and advance the infrastructure required for future fault-tolerant quantum systems. The initiative supports the U.S. Department of Energy's Quantum Genesis Mission and its goal of enabling scientifically relevant quantum computing by 2028.

title: Oak Ridge National Laboratory, IBM, and AMD launch co-design platform for quantum error correction
summary: Quantum error correction (QEC) is an important pillar of scientifically relevant quantum computing. Its value comes from what it unlocks: larger, deeper, and more capable quantum computations. The question is no longer if it’s possible - the challenge now is how to best enable quantum computers and classical high-performance computing (HPC) systems to work together to scale it. Quantum error correction (QEC) is an important pillar of scientifically relevant quantum computing. Its value comes from what it unlocks: larger, deeper, and more capable quantum computations. The question is no longer if it’s possible - the challenge now is how to best enable quantum computers and classical high-performance computing (HPC) systems to work together to scale it.In response to meet this challenge, the U.S. Department of Energy’s Quantum Science Center (QSC) at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), IBM, and @AMD have unveiled a new co-design platform for quantum error correction, with its initial deployment in IBM’s quantum facility in New York: https://www.ibm.com/quantum/blog/ornl-amd-error-correction-co-design-platform Engineered to help researchers advance quantum error correction techniques within the workflows they will ultimately support, the co-design platform pairs IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2 processors with ORNL’s Umbra high-performance computing (HPC) system, which is comprised of AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs and AMD Turin CPUs. These systems form a co-located environment that is connected to ORNL’s broader supercomputing ecosystem.

title: Cabinet Approves Vistar To Bring AI And Machine Learning Into India Statistics
summary: The Cabinet has approved the VISTAR scheme to improve statistical data and prepare national infrastructure for AI applications. This central sector initiative, titled the Viksit Bharat Initiative for Statistical Transformation, Analytics & Research, is set to run from 2026-27 to 2030-31 with an outlay of Rs 4,371.10 crore. The program focuses on standardizing statistical data to support the growing requirements of machine learning models. Beyond technical upgrades, the plan includes preparations for the eighth economic census and integrating mobile and e-commerce data to complement traditional survey methods. For policymakers and analysts, the scheme represents a shift toward using digital sources for more accurate national reporting. By consolidating these inputs, the government aims to build a robust framework that serves both research and industrial needs. title: Why AI Agents Need Their Own 70,000-Year-Old Language Revolution (with Vijoy Pandey)
summary: In Episode #1041, Dr. Vijoy Pandey (SVP and General Manager of Outshift, Cisco's incubation engine) returns for a third visit to explain why multi-agent systems fail without anyone noticing. Agents from different vendors, clouds and organisations can now exchange perfectly valid messages, but connection is not cognition: they do not agree on what those messages mean. Vijoy's team analyzed multi-agent sessions from its own production deployments and from public traces, and found a cognitive failure in every single one. In this episode, he lays out the kinds of failure he sees and how fast they compound, introduces the open-source observability platform and protocols Outshift has shipped to catch and correct drift mid-task, details a record-breaking quantum network running on real New York City fiber, and explains why probabilistic AI software running on deterministic hardware is a mismatch worth fixing. Additional materials: https://www.superdatascience.com/1041

title: Inference Optimization with CoreWeave Mission Control Agent
summary: CoreWeave Mission Control Agent, built into the CoreWeave Console, helps teams get more useful work from the GPUs they already have. In this demo, we show how it traces a slow CoreWeave Dedicated Inference endpoint serving agentic traffic to KV cache pressure, then quantizes the model to NVFP4 and reshapes it from one replica to two on the same eight GB200 GPUs. Load tests verify each change, showing more than 3x the output throughput per GPU with no new hardware. ⏳Timestamps: 0:09 Introducing CoreWeave Mission Control Agent 0:25 A healthy endpoint that has outgrown its configuration 1:16 Asking Mission Control Agent to investigate 2:19 Root cause: KV cache pressure under agentic traffic 3:03 Quantizing the model to NVFP4 on the same GPUs 4:09 Reshaping to two replicas at TP4 5:20 Load test results and applying TP4 7:37 More than 3x output per GPU on the same hardware

title: Using AI Won't Save Your Job
summary: Everyone says learn AI and you'll be safe. I think that skips the part where your company decides what to do with all your new speed. I keep hearing that people who use AI will win and everyone else will lose. Getting faster could help you take on better work and earn more, or it could mean your company keeps fewer people around. Both are possible. So I'd want people who trust my work, skills another employer would pay for, and maybe customers of my own. None of that is a guarantee. If your company didn't need you tomorrow, where could you take what you know?
